sources.title: P4 Advanced Financial Management September/December 2016 - Official Answers
sources.use: Project duration and a worked selling-price sensitivity margin.
sources.finding: Duration is calculated as the PV-weighted average time. Selling-price headroom is NPV divided by the discounted, post-tax revenue cash flows affected.
sources.formula: Duration = Σ(t × PV_t) / ΣPV_t; selling-price sensitivity = NPV / PV of affected post-tax revenue cash flows.

sources.title: AFM September/December 2019 - Official Sample Answers
sources.use: Second, very explicit AFM project-duration calculation.
sources.finding: The answer totals PV × time and divides by total positive PVs, producing 3.04 years.
sources.formula: Project duration = total (PV × time) / total PV.

sources.title: F9 June 2016 Examiner’s Report
sources.use: Black-and-white statement of the general sensitivity formula.
sources.finding: The denominator must be the present value of the project variable affected, after relevant tax effects.
sources.formula: Sensitivity % = 100 × NPV / PV of project variable.

sources.title: FM September/December 2023 Examiner’s Report
sources.use: Current ACCA convention for variable sensitivity and discount-rate sensitivity.
sources.finding: For the discount rate, IRR minus the original rate is the absolute headroom in percentage points. ACCA says percentage sensitivity divides that change by the original rate.
sources.formula: Variable sensitivity % = NPV / PV of affected post-tax variable × 100. Discount-rate sensitivity % = (IRR − original discount rate) / original discount rate × 100.

sources.title: AFM March/June 2019 - Official Sample Answers
sources.finding: The answer identifies an 11% project-specific risk-adjusted cost of capital based on a proxy company asset beta, then discounts the project cash flows at 11%.
sources.formula: Use the project-specific RADR as the discount rate applied to the project’s relevant cash flows.

sources.title: FM March/June 2018 - Official Sample Answers
sources.use: Joint-probability ENPV table and ACCA explanation of RADR derivation.
sources.finding: The official answer constructs joint probabilities and ENPV, and explains that a proxy beta can be ungeared and regeared to obtain a project-specific discount rate.
sources.formula: ENPV = Σ(probability × outcome NPV); RADR may be derived through CAPM using a proxy beta ungeared and regeared.

sources.title: F9 June 2015 - Official Answers
sources.finding: The answer calculates an expected input using probabilities, carries it through the project cash-flow table, and labels the result ENPV.
sources.formula: Expected input = Σ(probability × outcome); ENPV is the NPV based on probability-weighted expected inputs/outcomes.

sources.title: AFM September 2018 - Official Answers (Airone / Washi Co)
sources.use: Calculator #11 (fxhedge.ts) FIX ROUND 2, 2026-07-23 - per-unit currency option premium formula, cited by the GPT adjudication round and independently re-verified here by direct fetch.
sources.finding: The official answer computes the option premium as a flat per-unit rate multiplied by the number of contracts and contract size, with NO time proration applied - confirming the FIX ROUND 1 K3 correction (an earlier engine version wrongly prorated by months/12, an unsourced import from an interest-rate-options formula).
sources.formula: Premium payable = premium per unit × contract size × number of contracts (worked: JPY 3.8 × 125,000 × 640 = JPY 304m).

sources.title: AFM March/June 2021 Examiner's Report (currency futures/options hedge question)
sources.use: Calculator #11 (fxhedge.ts) FIX ROUND 2, 2026-07-23 - full worked lock-in-rate calculation, cited by the GPT adjudication round ("MJ21") and independently re-verified here by direct fetch. Algebraically checked against the engine's own formula and found to be an EXACT match under a sign-convention transposition (see finding).
sources.finding: The report's own convention defines basis = opening futures price − spot rate (the OPPOSITE sign to this engine's basis0 = spot0 − futures0), and its lock-in formula is 'opening futures price − basis remaining'. Substituting the sign-flip shows this is algebraically IDENTICAL to this engine's lock_in_rate = futures0 + unexpired_basis - both routes compute exactly 0.2374 US$/MR1 on the worked figures. Also confirms premium-currency conversion (not proration) is the graded error class the examiner flags, matching GATE 18's scope.
sources.formula: Worked: current basis = 0.2378 − 0.2358 = 0.0020; basis remaining = 0.0020 × 1/5 = 0.0004; lock-in rate = 0.2378 − 0.0004 = 0.2374 US$/MR1.

technical_articles.title: How to answer a foreign exchange risk management question (ACCA P4/AFM technical article)
technical_articles.note: Live HTML page, not a stable PDF - no byte-guard applies; verified by direct WebFetch 2026-07-23.
technical_articles.use: Calculator #11 (fxhedge.ts) FIX ROUND 2 - (a) confirms a RECEIPT is hedged by SELLING futures (the direction/instrumentSide convention), (b) a second per-unit premium example (quoted in cents, not the notional's own major unit), (c) a second, independently-worded lock-in-rate example.
technical_articles.finding: Nutourne Co (USA-based) receives CHF and hedges by SELLING CHF futures — confirms the receipt-sells / payment-buys direction convention. Separately shows a premium quoted as 0.86 US cents per CHF unit (a currency-denomination nuance: the premium's quote currency need not match the notional's major-unit convention). A second lock-in-rate worked example (1.0369 − 0.0011 = 1.0358) is ALGEBRAICALLY the same formula as T1, confirming it is not a one-off phrasing.
technical_articles.formula: Verbatim: "Sell CHF futures now to hedge against sale of CHF when money received from Swiss customer."; premium: "Multiply number of contracts × size of one contract × 0.0086, as premium is quoted in US cents (not US dollars) per CHF."

technical_articles.title: Interest rate risk management (ACCA P4/AFM technical article)
technical_articles.note: Live HTML page, not a stable PDF - no byte-guard applies; verified by direct WebFetch 2026-07-24.
technical_articles.use: Calculator #12 (IR hedging) Step-0 - the canonical IR-risk article: FRA rate-locking, futures direction/contract-count/premium worked example, the classic comparative-advantage swap (Titans FC / Kendri Co), and a bare mention of the collar.
technical_articles.finding: Part (a): borrower sells March futures to hedge a loan; contracts = notional/contract-size x loan-period/contract-period (40 contracts worked); a borrower's PUT option caps the rate ("MARCH PUT AT 94.000"); option premium = rate% x contracts x contract-size x contract-period/12 (WITH time proration - differs from the FX K3 all-in convention). Part (b): a full comparative-advantage swap between an absolute-advantage party (Titans FC) and a comparative-advantage party (Kendri Co), intermediated by a bank, saving split (fixed-rate-diff - floating-rate-diff) x 1/2 before fees, then each party nets a bank fee off their share. Collar mentioned only in passing: "reduce this cost by selecting to cap at a higher rate ... or using a collar hedge", sacrificing benefit if rates fall below the floor - NO worked collar example in this article.
technical_articles.formula: Contracts = $30m/$0.5m x 2mths/3mths = 40; premium = 0.255% x 40 x $500,000 x 3/12 = $12,750; swap saving = (3%-1%) x 1/2 = 1% pa excluding fees, then each party nets a 0.5% bank fee off their share.

technical_articles.title: How to answer an interest rate risk management question (ACCA P4/AFM technical article)
technical_articles.note: Live HTML page, not a stable PDF - no byte-guard applies; verified by direct WebFetch 2026-07-24.
technical_articles.use: Calculator #12 (IR hedging) Step-0 - the fullest worked depositor-side FRA/futures/options example found (D27,000,000 deposit), incl. the full futures expected-close-price mechanic through to net result under BOTH a rate-rise and a rate-fall scenario.
technical_articles.finding: Depositor buys futures ("Buy futures now (go long in the futures market), as the hedge is against a fall in interest rates") and buys CALL options ("Buy call options as need to hedge against a fall in interest rates"; exercise if strike below expected futures price). Contracts = notional/contract-size x deposit-period/contract-period (90 contracts worked). Basis = (100 - spot rate) - futures price; unexpired basis diminishes linearly by elapsed/total contract life (2/6 x 1.02 = 0.34). Expected closing futures price = 100 - expected rate - unexpired basis (NOT the FX lock-in-rate formula 'opening futures + unexpired basis' - the two families' formulas are structurally different because IR futures price = 100-rate while FX futures price is a currency rate). Gain/loss on futures = (closing price - opening price) x contract-size x contract-period/12 x contracts, netted against the money-market actual return/cost to give a net result and effective annual rate - reconciles to the SAME effective rate (4.58%) under both a rate-rise and a rate-fall scenario, confirming the hedge locks a single effective rate as designed.
technical_articles.formula: Contracts = D27,000,000/D500,000 x 5/3 = 90; basis = (100-4.20)-94.78 = 1.02; unexpired basis (31 Jan) = 2/6 x 1.02 = 0.34; expected futures price (rate=5.3%) = 100-5.3-0.34 = 94.36; futures gain/loss = (0.9436-0.9478) x D500,000 x 3/12 x 90 = (47,250); net result (both scenarios) = 515,250, effective annual rate 515,250/27,000,000 x 12/5 = 4.58%.

technical_articles.title: Basis risk (ACCA P4/AFM technical article)
technical_articles.note: Live HTML page, not a stable PDF - no byte-guard applies; verified by direct WebFetch 2026-07-24.
technical_articles.use: Calculator #12 (IR hedging) Step-0 - confirms the linear-diminishing-basis assumption used across T4/T5 is the general ACCA convention, not a one-off worked-example artefact, and flags it as a simplifying assumption ACCA itself calls out as not holding in practice (this is the standard scepticism-mark hook seen in the Northney/Sohbet examiner reports).
technical_articles.finding: "Basis is the difference between the futures and spot prices" and "basis is often assumed to diminish at a constant rate", explicitly flagged as a simplifying assumption that "may not hold true in practice" - the source of the basis-risk discussion/scepticism marks referenced in the Abertafol and Sohbet examiner reports (E1, E4).
technical_articles.formula: Basis = spot price - futures price = (100-4.20)-94.78 = 1.02; unexpired basis (31 Jan) = 2/6 x 1.02 = 0.34.

technical_articles.title: Determining interest rate forwards and their application to swap valuation (ACCA P4/AFM technical article, Nov 2011)
technical_articles.note: Live HTML page, not a stable PDF - no byte-guard applies; verified by direct WebFetch 2026-07-24. A byte-identical PDF companion (sa_nov2011_intrateswaps.pdf) was also fetched and cross-checked - same content.
technical_articles.use: Calculator #12 (IR hedging) Step-0 - the ONLY ACCA technical article on interest rate swaps beyond T4's comparative-advantage example. Uses a DIFFERENT presentation: deriving annual forward rates from a company's spot yield curve, then solving for the swap's fixed-equivalent rate by NPV-ing the net swap flows to zero.
technical_articles.finding: Bank offers to swap a company's variable-rate loan payments for a fixed rate: "the company pays a fixed rate of interest to the bank in exchange for receiving a variable rate of return from the bank based on the above yield rates less 50 basis points" (a bank margin/spread taken off the floating leg, not a flat fee as in T4). The fixed-equivalent rate R is solved by setting the NPV of (variable receipt - R) over the loan life to zero, discounting at the spot yield-curve rates. "In practice the receipts and payments of the swap would be netted off" - year-by-year net cash flow is receipt-or-payment depending on sign, not a single flat annual swap payment. AMBIGUITY: this NPV/forward-curve swap style and T4's comparative-advantage swap style are BOTH on ACCA's technical-articles page but structurally unrelated - neither the SD23/MJ25/SD24 examiner reports (Abertafol/Sohbet/Northney) feature a swap requirement at all, so there is no recent real-exam anchor confirming which style (or a third, simpler style) AFM currently examines.
technical_articles.formula: One-year forward rate = spot(2yr)^2 / spot(1yr) (e.g. 1.0460^2/1.0350 = 1.0571, i.e. 5.71%); swap fixed rate R solves Σ[(variable_t - R) x 100m] x discount_factor_t = 0 across the loan life.
